sections.title: Acute pancreatitis: definition, types and causes
sections.contentHtml:
Acute pancreatitis is acute inflammation caused by intrapancreatic activation of digestive enzymes, producing autodigestion.

TypeDescription
Acute edematousUsually mild and self-limited; peripancreatic fat necrosis with sparing of acinar cells
Hemorrhagic / necrotizingExtensive inflammation with coagulative necrosis of the gland and surrounding tissues
  • Common causes (90%): gallstones, alcohol, idiopathic and post-ERCP.
  • Rare causes: surgery, trauma, drugs such as azathioprine/thiazides, hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia, pancreas divisum, hereditary disease, renal failure, transplantation, mumps/coxsackie, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, severe hypothermia and petrochemical exposure.

sections.title: Clinical features, differential and complications
sections.contentHtml:
Classic presentation

Severe, constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, building over 15–60 minutes; nausea/vomiting; marked epigastric tenderness; quiet or absent bowel sounds as paralytic ileus develops.

  • Early guarding and rebound may be absent because inflammation is retroperitoneal.
  • Severe disease may cause hypoxia, hypovolemic shock and oliguria.
  • Grey Turner sign: flank discoloration; Cullen sign: periumbilical discoloration—features of hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
  • Differential diagnosis: perforated viscus, myocardial infarction and acute cholecystitis.
ComplicationMechanism in source
SIRS / shockCytokines, kinins, PAF, increased permeability, vomiting, ileus and renal failure
HypoxiaARDS due to pulmonary microthrombi
HyperglycemiaIslet disruption
HypocalcemiaCalcium sequestration in fat necrosis
AbscessInfection of necrotic tissue
Ascites / pleural effusion / pseudocystPancreatic-duct disruption
Variceal hemorrhageSplenic or portal-vein thrombosis
Duodenal obstruction / obstructive jaundiceCompression by pancreatic mass / common bile duct compression

sections.title: Diagnosis, imaging and severity
sections.contentHtml:
Diagnosis: at least 2 of 3
  1. 1
    Characteristic upper abdominal pain
  2. 2
    Amylase and/or lipase at least 3× the upper limit of normal
  3. 3
    Characteristic imaging findings
ModalityRole / limitation
UltrasoundInitial screening, especially gallstones and biliary obstruction; may be obscured by bowel gas
Contrast CTPreferred for defining necrosis, complications and severity; ideal after 48–72 hours in severe/equivocal cases
MRI / MRCPBiliary and ductal detail without radiation; useful when CT contrast is unsuitable
ERCPDiagnostic and therapeutic in obstructive biliary pancreatitis; invasive
Severity

Ranson scoring uses admission and 48-hour criteria. The lecture also emphasizes organ failure, shock, hypoxia, renal dysfunction and necrosis as severe features.

sections.title: Acute pancreatitis management
sections.contentHtml:
1. 1
    NPO in severe disease and provide nutrition as indicated in the lecture
  2. 2
    Analgesia
  3. 3
    Aggressive correction of hypovolemia with saline and/or colloids
  4. 4
    Correct electrolytes, especially calcium, magnesium and potassium
  5. 5
    Oxygen and ventilatory support if needed
  6. 6
    Treat complications; antibiotics for infected necrosis rather than routine sterile disease
  7. 7
    Address the cause, including biliary intervention when appropriate
Monitoring

Observe hemodynamics, urine output, oxygenation, organ failure, necrosis, abscess, pseudocyst and duct-related collections.

sections.title: Chronic pancreatitis and exocrine insufficiency
sections.contentHtml:
Chronic pancreatitis is a chronic inflammatory disease with fibrosis and destruction of exocrine tissue; diabetes occurs in advanced disease when the islets are involved.

  • Pain: recurrent acute-pancreatitis episodes in about 50%, or slowly progressive chronic pain in about 35%; may improve leaning forward and worsen with alcohol.
  • Exocrine failure: steatorrhea and maldigestion, usually after extensive loss of function.
  • Endocrine failure: diabetes in advanced disease.
  • Complications include pseudocyst, biliary/duodenal obstruction, portal or splenic-vein thrombosis, pancreatic ascites/effusion and malignancy risk noted in the lecture.
AssessmentSource role
CT / ultrasound / abdominal X-rayAtrophy, calcification, duct dilatation and pseudocyst
MRCP / ERCP / EUSDuctal and parenchymal assessment; EUS is sensitive for detailed change
Fecal elastase-1Most sensitive and specific indirect stool test in the lecture
Direct secretin/CCK testsAssess bicarbonate and enzyme secretion; reference standard but invasive
72-hour fecal fatDocuments steatorrhea / maldigestion

passages.title: Pancreas Anatomy
passages.text:
DISEASES OF THE PANCREAS
Pancreas Anatomy
✓ The pancreas is an elongated, tapered organ located across the back of the abdomen, behind
the stomach.
✓ The right side of the organ (called the head) is the widest part of the organ and lies in the
curve of the duodenum.
✓ The tapered left side extends slightly upward (called the body of the pancreas) and ends near
the spleen (called the tail)
✓ The pancreas is made up of two types of tissue:
▪ Exocrine tissue
The exocrine tissue secretes digestive enzymes. These are secreted into a network
of ducts that join the main pancreatic duct, which runs the length of the pancreas.
▪ Endocrine tissue
The endocrine tissue, which consists of the islets of Langerhans, secretes
hormones into the bloodstream.

passages.title: WHAT IS PANCREATITIS?
passages.text:
WHAT IS PANCREATITIS?
Pancreatitis is an inflammatory process in which pancreatic enzymes auto digest the gland
Normally, digestive enzymes do not become active until they reach the small intestine, where
they begin digesting food.
✓ But if these enzymes become active inside the pancreas, they start "digesting" the pancreas
itself
✓ The gland can sometimes heal without any impairment of function or any morphologic
changes.
o This process is known as acute pancreatitis.
o It can recur intermittently, contributing to the functional and morphologic loss of
the gland → Recurrent attacks are referred to as chronic pancreatitis.
✓ Acute pancreatitis occurs suddenly and lasts for a short period of time and usually resolves.
✓ Chronic pancreatitis does not resolve itself and results in a slow destruction of the pancreas.
Acute pancreatitis
Definition
• Acute inflammation resulting from intrapancreatic activation of digestive enzymes
TYPES:
1. Acute edematous pancreatitis:
The pancreatic inflammation and disease is mild & self-limited in most patients with
peripancreatic fat necrosis but sparing acinar cells.
2. Hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis:
The inflammation may be extensive & progressing to coagulation necrosis of the
gland & the surrounding tissues
Epidemiology
✓ About 80,000 cases occur in the United States each year; some 20 percent of them are
severe.
✓ Acute pancreatitis occurs more often in men than women.

passages.title: Diagnosis of Acute Pancreatitis: Clinical Guidelines
passages.text:
Diagnosis of Acute Pancreatitis: Clinical Guidelines
1. The Diagnostic Criteria
A definitive diagnosis is generally made when at least two of the following are present:
1. Clinical: Characteristic upper abdominal pain.
2. Biochemical: Serum amylase or lipase ≥ 3 times the upper limit of normal.
3. Radiological: Evidence of pancreatic swelling or necrosis on Ultrasound or CT.
2. Laboratory Investigations
Enzyme Profiles
• Serum Amylase: Rises rapidly but may return to normal within 24–48 hours.
o Clinical Pearl: Persistent elevation suggests pseudocyst formation.
o Pancreatic Ascites: Amylase will be present in peritoneal fluid.
• Serum Lipase: More specific than amylase. It remains elevated for up to 12 days, making
it the preferred marker for late presentations or chronic-on-acute episodes.
• Urinary Amylase/Creatinine Ratio: Useful if serum amylase has already normalized.
Metabolic & Hematologic Markers
• CBC: Expect Leukocytosis (WBC > 12,000) with a shift to segmented polymorphs.
• CRP: Used for serial assessment to monitor the severity and inflammatory response.
• Hyperglycemia: Occurs due to beta-cell injury within the pancreatic islets.
• KFTs and Electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, Ca, P, Mg): Expect significant disturbances due to "third
spacing" of fluids.
• Calcium & Magnesium: Often decreased; monitoring is vital for prognosis.
• Liver Function Tests (ALT, AST, Alk Phos, Bilirubin): Transiently elevated, especially if
the etiology is biliary (gallstones).

passages.text:
RANSON SCALE
• Ranson developed a series of different criteria for the severity of acute pancreatitis
• For the following categories answer each question regarding the patient then add up
total score for prognosis
o If answer is no (o point)
o If answer is yes (1 point)
Present on admission
• Older than 55 years
• WBC higher than 16,000 per mcL
• Blood glucose higher than 200 mg/dL
• Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) more than 350 IU/L
• SGOT (ie, aspartate aminotransferase [AST]) greater than 250 IU/L
Developing during the first 48 hours
• Hematocrit fall more than 10%
• BUN increase more than 8 mg/dL
• Serum calcium less than 8 mg/dL
• Arterial oxygen saturation less than 60 mm Hg
• Base deficit higher than 4 mEq/L
• Estimated fluid sequestration higher than 600 mL
✓ A Ranson score of 0-2 has a minimal mortality rate.
✓ A Ranson score of 3-5 has a 10%-20% mortality rate.
✓ A Ranson score higher than 5 has a mortality rate of more than 50% and is associated with
more systemic complications.

passages.title: Management of Severe Acute Pancreatitis
passages.text:
Management of Severe Acute Pancreatitis
1. NPO (Nil Per Os) – Nothing by mouth. Provide parenteral nutrition.
2. Analgesia – Administer pethidine for pain control.
3. Fluid Resuscitation – Correct hypovolemia with normal saline and/or colloids.
4. Monitoring – Insert CVP line and urinary catheter to monitor shocked patients.
5. Oxygen Therapy – Administer O₂ for hypoxia.
6. Respiratory Support – ARDS may require ventilatory support.
7. Glycemic Control – Use insulin for hyperglycemia.
8. Calcium Supplementation – IV calcium if tetany occurs.
9. GI Decompression – Nasogastric aspiration for paralytic ileus.
10. Thromboembolism Prophylaxis – Low-dose SC heparin.
11. Biliary Obstruction – If cholangitis or jaundice present, perform urgent ERCP to
remove stones and drain biliary system.
12. Antibiotics – Administer prophylactic antibiotics as indicated.
TTT of complications:
1. Necrotizing pancreatitis or pancreatic abscess urgent surgical debridement of the
pancreas
2. Pancreatic pseudocysts drainage into stomach or duodenum
3. Pancreatic ascites is indication for distal pancreatectomy

passages.title: DIAGNOSIS OF EXOCRINE PANCREATIC INSUFFICIENCY
passages.text:
DIAGNOSIS OF EXOCRINE PANCREATIC INSUFFICIENCY
Exocrine pancreatic function is assessed by measuring the organ's ability to secrete bicarbonate
and digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, and proteases) in response to hormonal stimulation or
food intake.
1. Direct Functional Testing (The Gold Standard)
Direct tests involve the administration of exogenous hormones to stimulate the pancreas,
followed by the collection of duodenal juice via a tube.
• Secretin Stimulation: Secretin is introduced to observe the production of pancreatic
juice. A healthy response shows an increased volume of secretion and high bicarbonate
levels.
• Pancreozymin (CCK) Stimulation: This stimulates acinar cells to release enzymes. A
healthy response shows an increased concentration of enzymes (lipase, amylase,
trypsin).
• Clinical Significance: In cases of severe exocrine insufficiency, these tests show
pathological changes in 85–90% of patients.
2. Indirect Testing: Breath Tests (13C-Labeled)
These non-invasive tests measure the digestion and absorption of specific substrates by tracking
the exhalation of labeled CO2.

passages.title: 3. Laboratory & Stool Analysis
passages.text:
3. Laboratory & Stool Analysis
These methods are commonly used for initial screening and routine monitoring.
• Fecal Elastase-1: This is the most sensitive and specific indirect test. Unlike other
enzymes, elastase-1 is not degraded during intestinal transit, making it an accurate
marker of pancreatic output.
• Coprogram (Stool Microscopy): A visual and chemical analysis of the stool. Signs of
maldigestion include:
o Steatorrhea: Presence of neutral fats.
o Creatorrhea: High content of undigested muscle fibers, indicating a failure to
digest protein.
o Amylorrhea: Presence of undigested starch/fiber.
STANDARD OF NONINVASIVE DIAGNOSIS OF CHRONIC PANCREATITIS

PANCREATITIS, CHRONIC - CT SCAN
Plain X-ray of abdomen showing calcific pancreatitis
CT SCAN WITH CENTRAL PSEUDOCYST
Endoscopic ultrasound overcomes some of the visualization problems and is probably more
sensitive and specific. CT has a sensitivity of up to 90% and specificity of the same order. It will
detect variation in ductal diameter, and ectatic side branches, changes in the parenchyma,
calcification and complications of chronic pancreatitis such as pseudocyst formation

passages.text:
AN ENDOSCOPIC ULTRASOUND IMAGE DEMONSTRATING A DILATED PANCREATIC DUCT
(MARKERS) IN A PATIENT WITH ADVANCED CHRONIC PANCREATITIS
An endoscopic ultrasound, which allows a highly detailed examination of
the pancreatic parenchyma and pancreatic duct, routinely detects
abnormalities in patients with chronic pancreatitis (high sensitivity), but
the specificity and reproducibility of the test requires further study
INSTRUMENTAL DIAGNOSTICS
✓ Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP): reveals impaired patency of
the main and secondary ducts. “Chain of lakes" is a classic symptom of chronic
pancreatitis (areas of constriction and expansion of Wirsung's ducts). It is also possible
the segmental or total obstruction of a ductal system of pancreas.
✓ Biopsy of pancreas.
